studies.label: Laboratory team press-release experiment: unequal versus full AI access, with a common earlier no-AI baseline
studies.cluster_se_treatment: The AI-phase unadjusted comparisons use one score per randomized team. Table 1 instead fits OLS to repeated team-task submissions from both phases; no team-clustered or repeated-measures standard-error adjustment is stated. Its SEs are not printed. The arm cluster counts are the team counts in the baseline table (Table 3), not separately stated post-treatment counts.

arms.name: Unequal AI access
arms.description: Only one randomly selected member of each team could use Kimi during the treatment-phase AR-glasses press-release task. Access and team assignment were randomized (PDF p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2). Arm-specific people counts are not printed.

arms.name: Full AI access
arms.description: Both members of each team could use Kimi during the same treatment-phase AR-glasses press-release task (PDF p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2). Arm-specific people counts are not printed.

arms.name: No AI access (earlier common baseline)
arms.description: All teams first wrote an electric-bicycle press release without AI. This was the earlier task of the same participants, not a separately randomized arm, and must not be added to the study sample. The analyzed count denotes the common experimental sample, not a separately stated post-exclusion baseline total (PDF p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.1-3.3).

studies.task: Two-person teams collaboratively wrote a 700-character Chinese press release about an electric bicycle without AI, followed by an AR-glasses press release with their assigned Kimi access (PDF p. 6, Section 3.3).

ai_tool.name: Kimi 3.0 (Moonshot), as named in the paper
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.2; the model release year is not stated

estimates.outcome: Task quality: overall expert grade, unadjusted comparison
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Blinded marketing professionals assigned an overall grade from 1 to 7 based on writing quality, content quality, and originality. Each team submitted a jointly written press release; the grade is a task-quality measure, coded as usefulness.

sources.quote: task quality in teams with unequal AI access (M = 5.654, SD = 0.080)
and those with full AI access (M = 5.250, SD = 0.118), t = 2.881, p < 0.01.
Evaluators assigned an overall grade (1–7) to the writing task submissions based on three criteria: writing quality, content quality, and originality.

estimates.notes: The contrast is between randomized AI-access configurations during the treatment phase. One team-task submission supplies one outcome per randomized team, so the between-arm t-test counts clusters once (se_basis = cluster); sd_level = output refers to these team submissions. The prose labels the reported dispersions SD, whereas Figure 4 on PDF p. 9 says its error bars are standard errors of the mean. The SD labels and values are retained without relabeling or conversion; a reliable standardizer requires clarification. No degrees of freedom or analysis-specific people counts are printed for this test, and n_units is also left null. Table 3 gives baseline team counts, not explicit post-treatment analysis counts. Higher grades indicate better press-release quality, including originality. The adjusted regression is recorded separately.

estimates.outcome: Task quality: overall expert grade, covariate-adjusted OLS
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Blinded marketing professionals assigned an overall grade from 1 to 7 based on writing quality, content quality, and originality. Each team submitted a jointly written press release; the grade is a task-quality measure, coded as usefulness.

regression.model: Table 1, Model (1): OLS of task quality on no-access and full-access indicators, female proportion, team problem-solving ability, team creativity, and marketing experience, with unequal access as the reference category. Controls were collected before the tasks (PDF pp. 6 and 8, Sections 3.2 and 3.4.5). The printed coefficient is Full AI access minus Unequal AI access, hence control minus treatment under the extraction arm labels. The model includes the common earlier no-AI phase.

sources.locator: PDF p. 9, Table 1, Model (1), Full access to AI row
PDF p. 9, Table 1, significance and t-statistic footnote
PDF p. 9, Table 1, N row (first entry is Model (1))

sources.quote: Evaluators assigned an overall grade (1–7) to the writing task submissions based on three criteria: writing quality, content quality, and originality.

estimates.notes: The regression coefficient and t statistic retain their printed negative signs: the paper uses unequal access as its reference category, so these numbers express full minus unequal access. Do not interpret the negative coefficient as harm from unequal access. Table 1 labels its adjacent column SD, but the footnote calls these entries t statistics; the negative entry is recorded as t under that footnote, and no SE is inferred. The p-value bound follows the coefficient's two significance stars. The reported model N counts submission observations across the earlier no-AI and later AI tasks, not unique people or randomized teams. The methods describe repeated submissions from teams, and no correction for repeated team observations or team clustering is described, so se_basis is output and regression.se_type is not_stated. Means and SDs from the separate unadjusted comparison are not duplicated here. No standardized effect or analysis-specific people count is supplied.

estimates.outcome: Cognitive diversity between teammates' spoken contributions
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings of each member's concatenated, manually corrected spoken contributions, normalized to unit length. The outcome is cosine distance between the two teammates' vectors. It compares different people within a team, rather than final press releases across teams; larger distance indicates greater diversity. PDF p. 7, Section 3.4.3.

sources.quote: unequal AI access exhibited significantly higher cognitive diversity (M = 0.631, SD = 0.011) than those with full AI access (M = 0.510, SD = 0.018), t = 5.938, p < 0.01.

Cognitive diversity was then calculated as the cosine distance (d) between the normalized vectors of the two team members (i and j), with higher values of d indicating greater cognitive dissimilarity.

estimates.notes: The paper specifies independent-sample t-tests (PDF p. 8, Section 4.2). Each randomized team contributes one distance between its two members' aggregate spoken outputs in the AI phase, so unit is team and se_basis is cluster. sd_level = pair denotes the distribution of those non-overlapping teammate-pair distances, one per randomized team; it does not describe all possible participant pairs. The dispersions are transcribed as SD from the prose even though the Figure 4 caption on PDF p. 9 describes standard-error bars. No conversion is made. The test prints no degrees of freedom, analysis-specific people counts, or total count of analyzed pairs/teams, so those fields remain null. The PROCESS model sample size and baseline team counts are not substituted for the unadjusted test's sample size. Mediation-model direct paths adjusted for post-treatment interaction measures are excluded separately.

not_extracted.what: Task quality: AI versus No AI access (earlier common baseline)
not_extracted.reason: The no-AI task always preceded AI access and used a different product prompt; neither no-AI assignment nor condition order was randomized. The no-AI mean comparison and no-access OLS coefficient therefore do not provide an eligible AI-versus-no-AI contrast (PDF pp. 6, 8-9 and 14; Sections 3.2-3.3, 4.1 and 5.4; Table 1).

not_extracted.what: Cognitive diversity: AI versus No AI access (earlier common baseline)
not_extracted.reason: The unassisted discussion preceded AI use for every team, without randomized order. Its comparison with the later AI phase is an ineligible before-after contrast and is not after_ai evidence (PDF pp. 6 and 8-9, Sections 3.2 and 4.2).

not_extracted.what: Baseline task-quality balance comparison between eventual unequal- and full-access teams
not_extracted.reason: Table 3 reports the earlier common no-AI task, before the assigned assistance was provided, rather than an output produced with or after AI (PDF p. 10, Section 4.4.1; PDF p. 11, Table 3).

not_extracted.what: Baseline cognitive-diversity balance comparison between eventual unequal- and full-access teams
not_extracted.reason: These Table 3 means, dispersions, and test describe pretreatment discussions without AI, not an effect of the assigned AI access (PDF p. 10, Section 4.4.1; PDF p. 11, Table 3).

not_extracted.what: Task completion time, including unadjusted, OLS, and mediation results
not_extracted.reason: Elapsed task duration measures work process/efficiency, not creativity or diversity scored on the produced output. Mediation results also fall under the mediation exclusion (PDF p. 7, Section 3.4.2.2; PDF pp. 8-12, Sections 4.1-4.4.3, Tables 1-3 and Figures 4-7).

The paper re-runs a mediation model with originality as the outcome and reports mediator associations and a serial indirect effect. It prints no unadjusted arm means or eligible total arm contrast for originality (PDF pp. 10-11, Section 4.4.2; PDF p. 12, Figure 6). Mediation results are excluded by extraction rule 5.

not_extracted.what: Task-quality mediation and serial indirect effects
not_extracted.reason: The PROCESS mediation paths, mediator-outcome associations, and indirect effects are not eligible total contrasts between randomized AI arms. They condition on or decompose post-treatment cognitive diversity and interaction processes (PDF pp. 8-12, Sections 4.2-4.4.3, Table 2 and Figures 5-7). The total OLS comparison in Table 1 is retained separately.

not_extracted.what: Cognitive-diversity mediation-model direct paths and robustness specifications
not_extracted.reason: The direct AI-access paths in the PROCESS model adjust for post-treatment team interaction processes. These mediator-adjusted effects are excluded, including the originality and alternative interaction-concentration models (PDF pp. 8-12, Sections 4.2-4.4.3 and Figures 5-7). The unadjusted arm means and t-test are retained.

A team interaction-process mediator; treatment-phase effects are reported as paths in mediation models rather than eligible creativity/diversity outcome contrasts. Baseline descriptives are pretreatment (PDF pp. 7-12, Sections 3.4.4, 4.3.1 and 4.4.1, Table 3 and Figures 5-7).

A team interaction-process mediator, with treatment effects and serial mediation paths reported in the excluded PROCESS analyses; the baseline table is pretreatment (PDF pp. 7-12, Sections 3.4.4, 4.3.1 and 4.4.1, Tables 2-3 and Figures 5-7).

not_extracted.what: Concentrated task-related questioning, ratio and difference-score variants
not_extracted.reason: A team interaction-process mediator; its effects and pathways are reported within mediation models, and baseline balance results precede AI assistance (PDF pp. 8 and 10-12, Sections 3.4.4.2, 4.3.2 and 4.4.1-4.4.3, Tables 2-3 and Figures 5-7).

not_extracted.what: Concentrated task-related answering, ratio and difference-score variants
not_extracted.reason: A team interaction-process mediator; only mediation-model and pretreatment balance results are reported (PDF pp. 8 and 10-12, Sections 3.4.4.2, 4.3.2 and 4.4.1-4.4.3, Table 3 and Figures 5-7).

not_extracted.what: Self-assessed communication, creativity/originality, and problem-solving skills; demographic and experience balance checks
not_extracted.reason: These are pretreatment self-reports and control variables, not scores on creative output (PDF pp. 6 and 8, Sections 3.1-3.2 and 3.4.5; PDF p. 11, Table 3).

not_extracted.what: Writing quality and content quality as separate dimensions
not_extracted.reason: The dimensions contribute to the extracted overall expert task-quality grade, but no separate full-sample AI-arm outcome statistics are printed for either dimension (PDF pp. 6-7, Section 3.4.2.1; PDF pp. 10-11, Section 4.4.2).

not_extracted.what: Gender-based post-hoc comparisons of team processes/productivity
not_extracted.reason: Subgroup/moderation analyses are excluded; the paper gives only a verbal nonsignificance statement and no numerical full-sample contrast (PDF pp. 13-14, Section 5.4).

open_items: Confirm whether the dispersions labeled SD in Sections 4.1-4.2 (PDF pp. 8-9) are standard deviations or standard errors; Figure 4 calls its error bars standard errors. Until resolved, these printed SDs should not be treated as unambiguous standardizers.

Clarify the SD column in Table 1 (PDF p. 9). Negative entries and the t-statistic footnote support transcribing these as t statistics, but the header conflicts. No regression standard error or degrees of freedom is printed; neither is derived here.

Provide analysis-specific people counts and treatment-phase team/output counts for the unadjusted tests. Table 3 (PDF p. 11) provides baseline team counts only; arm people counts are absent and have not been obtained by multiplication. The study analyzed total retains the reported experimental sample; a separately labeled post-exclusion people total is not supplied.

Clarify how repeated team submissions are treated in the OLS uncertainty and what the PROCESS sample rows represent relative to the OLS rows (PDF pp. 8-11). The PROCESS count is not transferred to any extracted t-test, and the OLS observation count is not used as a people count.

The external supplement described in PDF pp. 6-7 and linked on PDF p. 14 was not on file. Its evaluator rubric, originality-score construction, and any additional results remain uninspected. urllib requests with the required User-Agent to both named Frontiers article URL forms failed with WinError 10013; no supplementary numbers were guessed.
The release year of Kimi 3.0 is not stated. The cited Kimi-VL technical report does not establish the release year of the product named in the experiment; ai_tool.year remains null.

Participant overlap with DOI 10.1002/pra2.1437 is not established by the saved PDF. The screening form leaves overlap unresolved; the citation record infers the same work from matching abstracts and lists the later proceedings publication, but does not confirm a formal version relationship. Avoid treating it as a verified independent sample without reconciliation.
notes: Extraction B from the saved full-length journal article. The complete markdown was read in contiguous chunks through the references; there is no appended supplement or appendix. All quoted pages were checked with PyMuPDF, all tables were recovered with find_tables, and all embedded figures were inspected in memory. Eligible statistics occur in Section 4.1 (task-quality means, printed SDs and t-test), Table 1 Model (1) (adjusted AI-arm coefficient, t statistic under the table footnote, p bound and model observation count), and Section 4.2 (cognitive-diversity means, printed SDs and t-test). Figure 4 has no numeric data labels; no values were estimated from bar heights or error bars. Additional paths in Figures 5-7 are mediation results and were not extracted or read into numeric fields. Table 2 contains excluded indirect effects; Table 3 supplies baseline balance statistics and the study arm team counts. The only eligible randomized contrast is Unequal AI access versus Full AI access. The earlier common no-AI phase is not an independently randomized arm and does not create another sample. No number was standardized, sign-reversed, or derived from another statistic. Study people counts retain the reported experimental sample without adding expert raters or repeated outputs; estimate people counts remain null because they are not printed for the relevant analysis. Quotes normalize PDF whitespace only, preserving printed signs and precision.
